blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Detailed hand and foot articulation is important for animation and motion analysis, yet remains challenging to recover from monocular video. Recent expressive video methods infer hand articulation from shared whole-body representations. Our conference work suggests that this underexploits local evidence: the Foot Motion Refinement (FootMR) module refines ankle rotations from foot keypoints, improving reconstruction even when the initial estimator receives the same keypoints. We extend this principle to hands with the Hand Motion Refinement (HandMR) module. Because 2D finger keypoints are often missing or unreliable, HandMR combines image features of a pretrained hand reconstruction model with initial arm and hand rotations to refine elbows, wrists, and fingers. We integrate FootMR and HandMR into ExMR (Extremity Motion Refinement), a system for reconstructing 3D body, hand, and foot motion from monocular video. An initial temporal estimator predicts whole-body motion, after which both refiners revisit local evidence to predict residual joint rotations. Experiments on ARCTIC, MOYO, RICH, and MOOF show that ExMR outperforms state-of-the-art methods in hand and foot reconstruction, reducing hand per-vertex error and ankle joint angle error on MOYO by 19% and 18%, respectively, relative to the strongest competitor. Code will be made available for research purposes. Project page: https://twehrbein.github.io/exmr-website/
blocks.zh: 详细的手和脚表达对于动画和运动分析很重要,但从单相机视频中恢复仍然具有挑战性. 近期的表达式视频方法推断出来自共享全身表达的手语表达. 我们的会议工作表明,这种对本地证据的挖掘不足:脚运动精准化(FootMR)模块精炼出脚键点的脚踝旋转,即使初始估计器得到相同的键点,也改善了重建. 我们把这一原则推广到手动改进模块。 由于2D指键点往往缺失或不可靠,HandMR将预训手部重建模型的图像特征与起步臂和手自转来细化肘,手腕和指. 我们把FootMR和HandMR整合到ExMR(Extremity Motion Finement)中,这是一个从单相机视频中重建3D体,手和脚运动的系统. 一个初始的时间估计器预测了全身运动,之后两个精炼者都会重新审视当地的证据来预测残余的联合旋转. 有关ACTIC,MOYO,RICH,MOOF的实验显示,与最强的竞争对手相比,ExMR在手部和脚部重建方面都超越了最先进的方法,将MOYO的手部相向倒数误差和脚踝相向角误差分别减少19%和18%. 守则将提供给研究。 项目网页:https://twehrbein.github.io/exmr-website/

blocks.en: I Introduction
blocks.zh: 一. 导言

blocks.en:
Monocular human motion capture aims to recover a person’s 3D
movement from a single video, making motion reconstruction accessible for
applications such as animation, motion analysis, and AR/VR.
The motion of the extremities carries particularly important details:
ankle articulation contributes to lifelike dance animation, while wrist and finger
configurations convey how a hand grasps or manipulates an object.
Nevertheless, most current motion-capture methods primarily target overall body
motion [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] ,
and recovering detailed hand and foot articulation remains challenging.

Single-image expressive estimators [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] and per-frame body–hand integration methods [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] recover articulated hands with body context, but cannot exploit neighboring frames
to resolve pose ambiguities.
Hand-only video
methods [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] instead
use temporal evidence, but estimate the hand in isolation from the
articulated body that constrains it.
Expressive video methods such as WHAC [ 16 ] ,
Motions as Queries [ 17 ] , and
Human3R [ 18 ] combine body and temporal evidence
to recover body motion and hand articulation jointly.
However, all three extract hand evidence from
person crops or full video frames, where the small image area of the hands
can limit the available visual detail [ 19 ] .
Closest to our work, concurrent DanceHMR [ 20 ] instead
fuses separately encoded body and specialist hand observations before a
shared temporal encoder.
After fusion, temporal modeling of body motion and hand articulation
relies exclusively on a shared whole-body representation, which receives the
hand observations only once, before an explicit estimate of the arms and hands
exists.

blocks.en:
In our 3DV 2026 conference paper [ 21 ] , we introduced the
Foot Motion Refinement module (FootMR), which predicts residual ankle rotations
in a dedicated temporal network using local 2D foot keypoints, knee rotations,
and initial ankle rotations.
The paper showed that dedicated temporal refinement improved foot
reconstruction even when the initial temporal estimator already received the
same local evidence.
This finding motivates our hypothesis that fine-grained hand evidence
can remain underexploited in a shared whole-body representation.
We therefore investigate whether a
dedicated temporal stage can exploit the same hand observations more
effectively by revisiting them together with the arm and hand rotations of an
initial whole-body estimate and predicting residual joint rotations.
Learning corrections relative to an explicit estimate is
well established in single-image pose and mesh
recovery [ 22 , 23 , 19 ] .
Residual refinement has also been explored in video-based body reconstruction [ 24 ] ,
including separate temporal networks for body regions in
Local Recurrent Models (LMR) [ 25 ] .
In our hand-refinement stage, the initial arm and hand rotations can
summarize broader body and temporal context absent from an individual hand
crop. Additionally, they can provide a useful prior when the local
evidence is ambiguous, for example, under occlusion.

blocks.en:
Building on this refinement principle,
we introduce ExMR ( Extremity Motion Refinement ), a system for
reconstructing body, hand, and foot motion from monocular video.
Its initial estimator extends the GVHMR-based [ 3 ] estimator
of our conference paper and fuses body and specialist hand
image features before temporal modeling to predict SMPL-X
motion [ 26 ] with articulated hands.
FootMR and
the newly introduced Hand Motion Refinement module (HandMR) then refine the
initial motion sequence by predicting residual joint rotations in dedicated temporal networks.
We retain FootMR’s architecture and refinement
formulation and train both refiners jointly with the initial estimator.
FootMR and HandMR instantiate a common temporal residual-refinement
principle: revisiting local evidence together with explicit initial joint rotations
to predict corrections over time.
Fig. 1 shows ExMR’s reconstructions of a dance
sequence, with close-ups highlighting the recovered foot and hand
articulation.

blocks.en:
Adapting refinement to hands changes both the correction targets and the observations.
Hand refinement must account for a wrist and multiple finger joints per hand, compared with
one ankle rotation per side for foot refinement. A direct analog of FootMR would use
2D finger keypoints, but these are frequently missing or unreliable under self-occlusion
or occlusion by interacting objects. HandMR therefore uses latent
image features from HaMeR [ 27 ] , a pretrained model for 3D
hand reconstruction.
Extracted from local hand crops, these features can retain
cues beyond explicit keypoint coordinates. HandMR reuses the HaMeR features supplied
to the initial estimator, combining them with initial arm–hand rotations to
jointly refine elbows, wrists, and fingers.

blocks.en:
For feet, the design of FootMR was originally motivated by inaccurate foot
annotations and limited foot-motion diversity in the training data available
at the time of our conference work. Its keypoint representation permits
training on projected 3D motion without paired images and supports extensive
data augmentation. Advances in training data and image features could now
reduce the need for dedicated ankle refinement. BEDLAM2 [ 28 ] provides large-scale,
diverse synthetic video with ground-truth body motion, and
SAM3D-Body [ 9 ] explicitly
targets accurate body, hand, and foot reconstruction. We therefore strengthen the
inherited body-and-foot system by adopting SAM3D-Body image features, revising its
training mixture and objectives, and updating its test-time keypoint detector.
Matched comparisons with and without FootMR test whether dedicated foot refinement
remains beneficial.

blocks.en:
Relative to our conference paper, this journal article makes three main
contributions: • We introduce HandMR within ExMR, extending our conference
body-and-foot motion-capture system to articulated hands.
HandMR follows FootMR’s principle of predicting residual joint
rotations in a dedicated temporal network. To adapt this principle to articulated
hands, HandMR combines specialist hand image features with initial joint rotations
to jointly correct elbow, wrist, and finger articulation. • ExMR achieves the lowest hand reconstruction errors among
the compared methods on all three hand benchmarks.
HandMR substantially improves hand reconstruction over an otherwise
identical ExMR variant trained without it.
We further analyze hand-evidence representations, initial joint-rotation
conditioning, temporal accuracy and stability, and how refinement gains
vary with wrist articulation. • ExMR outperforms all compared competitors on every
reported foot metric across the three foot benchmarks.
We show in matched comparisons that the inherited FootMR module
improves foot reconstruction under the stronger body-and-foot configuration.
A cumulative revision analysis traces the complete system’s improvement
over the conference configuration.

blocks.en: II Related Work
blocks.zh: 二. 相关工作

blocks.en: II-A Single-Image Human Mesh Recovery
blocks.zh: II-A 单一图像人类网格恢复

blocks.en:
Single-image human mesh recovery commonly estimates the parameters of a
statistical body model from an RGB image. SMPL [ 32 ] provides
a compact representation of body pose and shape.
SMPLify [ 33 ] fits SMPL to detected 2D keypoints, while
HMR [ 23 ] learns feed-forward parameter regression.
A substantial literature has since developed around SMPL-based body
reconstruction.
CLIFF [ 34 ] adds full-image bounding-box conditioning to account
for perspective effects, and HMR2.0 [ 35 ] improves visual representations with a large
vision transformer backbone.

expressive face, enabling joint body, hand, and face recovery.
AiOS [ 36 ] progressively refines body, hand, and face features
in a single network for expressive SMPL-X reconstruction.
SMPLer-X [ 7 ] and SMPLest-X [ 8 ] scale training data and transformer capacity for expressive reconstruction.

using a DINOv3-based image backbone [ 38 ] .
These single-image estimators cannot exploit neighboring frames to resolve

Their learned visual representations nevertheless provide useful per-frame
evidence for ExMR’s temporal reconstruction.

widely used for hand-only reconstruction.
HaMeR [ 27 ] scales transformer capacity and hand training
data, and WiLoR [ 40 ] combines hand localization with
MANO reconstruction and image-aligned refinement. These specialists provide
detailed local estimates, although self-occlusion and hand–object interaction

blocks.en:
Consistent body–hand reconstruction requires coordinating wrist orientation
with the arm pose while exploiting detailed local hand evidence.
One strategy reconciles separate body and hand predictions by adjusting the
arm pose during integration.
FrankMocap [ 10 ] compares direct copy-paste with
optimization-based fitting and learned integration that adjusts shoulder and
elbow rotations. PyMAF-X [ 11 ] uses elbow-twist
compensation to avoid unnatural wrist poses.
Hand evidence can also guide body and wrist estimation directly:
PIXIE [ 41 ] fuses body and hand features, and
Hand4Whole [ 42 ] combines body and metacarpophalangeal (MCP)
joint cues for wrist estimation.
Such guidance can reuse a pretrained hand specialist, as in
Hand4Whole++ [ 12 ] , which injects specialist features into a
frozen whole-body estimator to improve wrist orientation.
SAM3D-Body [ 9 ] instead uses geometric prompts to refine
the body prediction before integrating optional hand-crop predictions.
In the converse direction, body estimates guide local hand reconstruction
through localization or explicit pose conditioning:
ExPose [ 19 ] uses an initial body estimate to define part crops,
whereas HMR-Adapter [ 43 ] conditions a frozen hand
estimator on joint rotations along the root-to-wrist kinematic chain.
These approaches establish complementary roles for local hand evidence and
body-derived kinematic context in recovering compatible arm and hand
configurations.

Relative to GVHMR, we replace its HMR2.0 image feature [ 35 ] with the SAM3D-Body image feature, add the two HaMeR features, and extend the

estimator predicts the joint rotations and shape together with
weak-perspective camera parameters for each person crop. The
sequence-level shape β \beta is obtained by averaging the predicted shape coefficients
over all L L frames. Following
CLIFF, we convert the camera parameters to the
perspective-camera translation τ c ( l ) \tau_{c}^{(l)} for the full image, thereby
obtaining the initial camera-frame SMPL-X sequence. FootMR and HandMR

estimate nor the camera estimate changes during refinement.

blocks.en:
FootMR jointly refines the initial left and right ankle rotations using sparse
2D foot evidence. Although SMPL-X parameterizes each foot with an ankle and a
forefoot joint, we target only the ankle. It has the larger influence on
overall foot motion, and our prior study found only limited gains from
additionally refining the forefoot [ 21 ] . Four 2D keypoints
per foot—the ankle, big toe, small toe, and
heel—provide compact, direct geometric evidence for this target and can be
reliably detected by modern whole-body pose
estimators [ 57 ] . Moreover, to our knowledge, no
publicly available foot-specific monocular 3D pose model exposes image features

For each frame, FootMR receives these four 2D keypoints per foot, the
person bounding-box encoding, and the global rotations of both knees and
ankles. Only the ankle rotations are refined; the knee rotations provide
kinematic context. As in the initial estimator, keypoints deemed not visible
according to their detector confidence are set to zero after normalization.

blocks.en:
HandMR specializes the refinement principle for articulated hands. A direct
analog of FootMR would use detected 2D finger keypoints for each hand.
Although these keypoints provide detailed geometric evidence when visible,
parts of the fingers are frequently self-occluded or hidden by objects or the
other hand, making the corresponding detections missing or unreliable. We
therefore use image features from HaMeR [ 27 ] , a specialist
model trained on a large mixture of 2D- and 3D-annotated hand data and designed
for robust monocular 3D hand reconstruction.
We choose HaMeR because its transformer decoder provides a single
1024-dimensional output token per hand crop, which can be used directly
as input to our temporal networks. Compared with a coordinate-only
representation, its latent features retain richer image evidence and can
preserve cues about visibility and ambiguity under partial occlusion. Our ablation in
Table II shows that these features provide more effective
hand evidence than 2D finger keypoints in our complete pipeline.

blocks.en:
FootMR and HandMR are separate temporal networks that update disjoint joint
groups without sharing parameters. Each independently processes its own
evidence and part-specific predictions from the shared initial estimator.
Both networks instantiate the same
architectural blueprint, which we adopt from GVHMR [ 3 ] .

blocks.en:
Following GVHMR, dedicated MLPs first embed the part-specific evidence, the
person bounding-box encoding, and rotation conditions. FootMR combines its
embeddings through element-wise summation into a 256-dimensional token. For
HandMR, a shared learned projection independently maps each of the two
1024-dimensional HaMeR
feature vectors to 256 dimensions. The resulting embeddings are concatenated
into a 512-dimensional visual-evidence embedding and summed element-wise with
the 512-dimensional box and rotation embeddings to form a 512-dimensional
token. This larger token accommodates HandMR’s higher-dimensional hand evidence
and substantially larger set of conditioned rotations compared with FootMR’s
few 2D keypoints and joint rotations. In either network, all information for
both sides of the body is represented by a single token per frame. The token
sequence is processed by six transformer encoder layers with four attention
heads and Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) [ 74 ] . A two-layer MLP
with GELU activation maps each output token to all residual rotations for the
joint groups refined by the corresponding network.

blocks.en: IV-A 4 Test-Time Inputs and Preprocessing
blocks.zh: IV-A 4 试验时间输入和预处理

blocks.en:
Unless stated otherwise, we obtain ExMR’s 23 body-and-foot keypoints with
Sapiens2-1B [ 57 ] and treat detections with confidence
below 0.5 0.5 as missing. The detector can be replaced without retraining if it
provides the same 23-keypoint layout.
Camera intrinsics are approximated by setting the focal length to the
full-image diagonal and the
principal point to the image center [ 34 ] .
For benchmark sequences with 3D ground truth, we use ground-truth person boxes
and construct each hand box from the projected annotated SMPL or SMPL-X hand
joints. For MOOF, which lacks 3D ground truth, and for arbitrary demonstration
videos, we use detected person boxes. The hand boxes in these cases are
constructed from visible finger keypoints predicted by a whole-body 2D
detector, following HaMeR’s demo protocol.
The hand boxes are only used to define separate left- and right-hand crops for the fixed
HaMeR encoder. If no visible finger keypoints are detected for a hand, all
coordinates of the corresponding hand box are set to zero, producing an all-black
input crop for HaMeR. The resulting HaMeR feature is passed to the
initial estimator and HandMR without an explicit hand-visibility indicator.

blocks.en:
Like ExMR, DanceHMR [ 20 ] integrates image features from
hand crops into temporal expressive SMPL-X estimation. Its code and pretrained weights were not
publicly available at evaluation time, so we report its published results
separately and construct a DanceHMR-style fusion baseline. This baseline is
intended as a controlled architectural comparison of body–hand integration,
not a reproduction of the complete method. It shares ExMR’s training protocol and Sapiens2-1B
test-time detector and uses the same temporal-transformer backbone as
ExMR’s initial estimator. We retain DanceHMR’s HaMeR hand features, input
organization, and fusion operation, but replace its HMR2.0 body feature with
ExMR’s SAM3D-Body feature.
Separate encoders map the body, left-hand, and right-hand observations
to one per-frame token each. The body observation combines 17 2D body keypoints,
the SAM3D-Body feature, and the same person bounding-box encoding and relative
camera rotation as ExMR. Each hand observation combines 20 2D finger
keypoints, a HaMeR feature, and a separate hand-box encoding. An MLP fuses the
concatenated hand tokens, and its output is added to the body token before the
temporal transformer. ExMR’s initial estimator instead integrates both
HaMeR features directly into its per-frame token and uses 23 body-and-foot
keypoints. It receives neither 2D finger
keypoints nor separate hand-box encodings.

blocks.en: V Conclusion
blocks.zh: 五 结论

blocks.en:
ExMR combines whole-body motion estimation with dedicated temporal refinement
of the hands and feet. It extends our conference body-and-foot system with HandMR,
which combines specialist hand image features with initial arm–hand rotations to
refine elbows, wrists, and fingers. Paired with FootMR’s
keypoint-based ankle refinement, this yields a jointly trained system
for reconstructing body, hand, and foot motion from monocular video.
FootMR and HandMR follow a common principle: revisiting local
observations together with explicit joint estimates to predict residual rotation
corrections over time.
Across the evaluated benchmarks, ExMR outperforms all competitors on
hand and foot reconstruction while achieving competitive body accuracy.
The experiments also show that how local evidence is used matters beyond its availability.
In matched comparisons, adding the HandMR and FootMR modules improves hand and foot
reconstruction even though the initial estimator already receives the same evidence.
These findings suggest that dedicated temporal refinement improves extremity reconstruction
by exploiting local evidence underused by a shared whole-body representation.

blocks.en:
The top block of Table S4 compares FootMR’s
joint-rotation inputs. Supplying initial ankle rotations also changes prediction
from direct regression to residual refinement. Both the ankle-only and knee-only
variants achieve lower AJAE on MOYO and RICH than the variant without rotation

reducing MOYO AJAE from 29.2 ∘ 29.2^{\circ} to 20.0 ∘ 20.0^{\circ} and RICH AJAE from 19.4 ∘ 19.4^{\circ} to 12.8 ∘ 12.8^{\circ} .
Adding hip and pelvis rotations yields no further improvement.
These results suggest that the initial ankle estimate provides a useful prior
and that global knee orientations contribute complementary kinematic context
for lifting the 2D foot-keypoint sequence to 3D.
